text: Eighty-one today. The grandchildren rang one after another. Margaret made a cake with far too many candles. A good day, all told.
The house is very quiet now that Bill is gone. I talk to the radio. It doesn't answer, but it helps.
Managed the stairs to the library without stopping. Six months ago I couldn't. The physiotherapist would be pleased.
Pension came in. Paid the gas, the phone, and put a little by for Christmas presents.
The new doctor didn't look up from his screen once. I might as well not have been in the room.
Sat in the garden with my tea and watched the blue tits on the feeder for an hour. Lovely and still.
Doris from church hasn't been for three Sundays. Rang her daughter. She's in hospital. I'll go Tuesday.
Our sixtieth anniversary would have been today. I put on the brooch he gave me and went to the seaside like we always did.
The young man next door carried my shopping up again and wouldn't take a penny. Such a kind lad.
Can't make head nor tail of the online banking. Three times I've been locked out. I want a person, not a password.
Gerald and I have started playing chess on Thursdays at the day centre. He cheats. I let him.
Thinking about the war again. Funny how it comes back at this age. Sixty years and I can still smell the station.
Great-grandson born this morning. Arthur, after my father. I wept into the telephone.
Very tired today. The new tablets make me sleepy. Dozed through the afternoon film.
My daughter wants me to move into the home near her. I know she means well. I'm not ready to leave my house.
Finished the jumper for Lily. Took me all winter with these hands. She'll grow out of it in a month.
Another funeral. Ted this time. There are so few of us left from the old street.
Bus pass renewed. Went into town for the first time in weeks. Bought a new hat. Felt quite the thing.
I'm grateful for my eyesight still being good enough to read. A book a week, still.
The council have closed the day centre on Fridays. That was my only outing. What am I to do with Fridays now?
Fell in the kitchen. Nothing broken, the paramedic said, just bruised pride. Pressed the button on my pendant like they told me to.
Can't remember if I took my morning pills. Counted them twice. This happens more now and it frightens me.
Looking forward to Sunday. The whole family is coming for lunch. I've already planned the roast.
Spoke to nobody today. Not a soul. The phone didn't ring once.
Planted the sweet peas along the fence like Mother used to. They'll be up by June if the slugs behave.
Angry with the gas company. They've doubled my bill and I can't get a human on the phone. I'm 84, not a website.
Granddaughter showed me how to video call. I saw Rajan's face in Australia for the first time in a year. Couldn't stop smiling.
Long, flat day. Rain, crosswords, soup. Not unhappy. Just long.
I've outlived three doctors, two dogs and a husband. Sometimes I wonder what I'm still here for. Then the grandchildren visit and I know.
Choir sang at the cathedral. My voice isn't what it was but I held the alto line. Very proud.
The nurse, Ama, sat with me for twenty minutes even though she was busy. Talked about her children. I felt like a person.
Tired in my bones. Eighty-seven is a lot of years to carry around.
Wrote letters to all the grandchildren for their birthdays this year. Twelve of them. A whole afternoon. Satisfied.
Hospital appointment changed for the third time. They wrote to the wrong address. I'm not cross, I'm just tired of it.
Found Frank's letters from when he was at sea. 1958. 'My dearest girl.' Read them all twice.
The young people at the bank were very patient today. Helped me set up the card on my phone. I'm quite modern now.
Peaceful morning. Wireless on low, porridge, the sun on the kitchen table.
The boy across the road shouts at his mother and I can hear it through the wall. It makes me so angry and so sad.
Everyone asks how I'm keeping. I say 'mustn't grumble'. I'd like to grumble just once.
Granddad's watch, which I've had in a drawer for forty years, is ticking again thanks to the man at the market. It felt like hearing his heart.
The family photo from the wedding is on the mantelpiece. Four generations. I'm in the middle, like a tree.
Hopeful the new hearing aids will help at the bridge club. I miss half the bidding.
Too many appointments this week. Eyes, feet, blood. My calendar is busier than when I worked.
Can't sleep. Lay awake thinking about whether I'll be a burden to the children.
Bert down the road won the marrow competition again. Mine was bigger. The judges are blind.
Moved into the flat at Willow Court. Smaller, warmer, a lift. Unpacked my books first. It might do.
Missing Kathleen. Fifty years of friendship and now just the space where her phone calls were.
Excited for the coach trip to the Lakes next week. Packed already. Sandwiches will be made Wednesday.
I am so grateful to still be in my own home at ninety. Not many get that.
Thinking about what I'll leave behind. Not money, there isn't much. Recipes, stories, the way I fold the sheets.
Lunch club cancelled again. Sat with the cat and a tin of soup instead.
Had a lovely chat with the girl at the pharmacy about her wedding. Brightened my week.
The children argued over my will in front of me. As if I'm already gone. Furious, and ashamed of them.
Took my first dance class at seventy-six. Ballroom. My partner, Clive, has two left feet. So do I.
Dozed in the chair after lunch, woke at four, didn't know what day it was. Getting old is odd.
Ordinary Wednesday. Library, post office, chemist. Home by noon.
Mr. Achterberg next door is in hospice now. We've waved over the fence every morning for thirty years.
The new curate asked me to read at the Sunday service. Haven't done that since 1979. Practising in front of the mirror.
Grateful for the warm-space scheme at the library. Free tea, company, and the heating on.
Calm, steady week. Nothing hurt too much and nobody died. At my age that's a good week.
My son only phones when he wants something. Today he wanted the car. I said yes. I always say yes.
Proud of Ellen for finishing her nursing degree at fifty-two. My girl. Never too late.
The cataract operation went well. The colours! I'd forgotten the curtains were green.
Can't keep up with the forms for Ivor's care. Every office wants a different one and they all want it yesterday.
I think I've made my peace with not going back to Jamaica. The memories will have to do. And they do.
Took the bus to the coast on my own. Sat on a bench with chips. Brave old thing.
Weekly shop delivered. Tins, bread, milk, biscuits for when Nora visits.
Not looking forward to winter. Dark by four, damp in the bones, and the long evenings alone.
The grandkids built a den in my living room and refused to leave it. Cushions everywhere. Glorious mess.
Thinking of Mum today. She'd have been a hundred and five. I still use her rolling pin.
